No biological endpoint data are reported; the work is limited to beam characterization and machine engineering.

contradictions.explanation: The paper proposes a specific radical-chemistry mechanism (peroxyl radical recombination reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation) coupled with NRF2 pathway activation as sufficient to explain sparing in this model, which qualifies the registered claim that oxygen depletion alone is insufficient by offering an alternative or complementary redox-based mechanism rather than addressing oxygen depletion directly.

The abstract states tumor control comparable to CONV-RT, consistent with the registered claim, but the finding that a substantially reduced FLASH dose can still achieve sparing while presumably maintaining tumor control (given a total dose threshold) adds nuance about dose-dependence not captured in the original claim.

key_findings: A reduced FLASH dose still elicits normal-tissue sparing provided a total dose threshold is met
FLASH-RT enhances peroxyl radical recombination, lowering oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation compared to CONV-RT
Antioxidant interventions implicate free radicals as mechanistically essential to the sparing effect
FLASH-RT activates the NRF2 antioxidant pathway and suppresses ERK signaling, reducing apoptosis and tissue injury
Tumor control is reported as comparable between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT
42002152.reviewer_note: Abstract omits beam quality, specific dose values, dose rates, and pulse structure, limiting assessment of relevance to BIO-001 and BIO-002 dose-rate threshold claims; full text would be needed to check whether reported dose-rate/time conditions align with or challenge those thresholds.
42002152.summary: This study uses a murine acute intestinal toxicity model and a tumor control model to examine how beam parameters influence FLASH sparing, combining FLASH-RT and CONV-RT irradiation with kinetic simulations, oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation measurements, antioxidant interventions, RNA sequencing, and NRF2 knockout mice. The authors report that a substantially reduced FLASH dose can still produce the sparing effect provided a total dose threshold is met. Kinetic simulation and experimental validation indicate that FLASH-RT enhances peroxyl radical recombination, reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, and antioxidant interventions confirm a role for free radicals in the effect. Molecular profiling shows that FLASH-RT activates the NRF2 antioxidant pathway while suppressing ERK signaling, reducing apoptosis and mitigating radiation-induced tissue injury. Specific beam energy, dose values, and dose rates are not given in the abstract.

key_findings: Permanent magnet synchrotron design with racetrack geometry and combined nonlinear field magnets achieves fixed betatron tunes across 10-250 MeV.
Target dose rate specification: 40 Gy/s delivered within 100 ms.
Facility footprint of 7 x 11 m2 with reduced expected operating cost due to permanent magnets.
Measured 28 MeV beam: 7.45 mm beam width (H and V), 6.5 mm Bragg peak depth, 8.97 mm peak gap.
42004839.reviewer_note: No biological or dosimetric-correction claims are tested here; the 40 Gy/s figure is stated as a design target consistent with BIO-002's dose-rate threshold but is not an independent test of that claim. This is an accelerator engineering and beam characterization report, appropriately placed in Beam Delivery & Technology despite some overlap with Physics & Dosimetry due to the reported beam profile measurements.
42004839.summary: This paper describes the design of a Bragg-peak FLASH proton irradiator built around a fixed-magnetic-field permanent magnet synchrotron, planned for installation at Stony Brook University Hospital. The racetrack-shaped accelerator uses combined nonlinear field magnets in its arcs to maintain fixed betatron tunes across a kinetic energy range of 10-250 MeV, targeting delivery of 40 Gy/s within 100 ms, and is designed to fit a 7 x 11 m2 footprint. As an initial physical characterization step, the authors measured a 28 MeV proton beam, reporting a beam width of 7.45 mm (horizontal and vertical), a Bragg peak depth of 6.5 mm, and a peak gap of 8.97 mm. The authors note this low-energy beam distribution is suited to planned small-animal studies.

key_findings: Electron beams, widely used in preclinical FLASH research, have penetration depth limitations that make them unsuitable for most stereotactic radiosurgery/SBRT applications.

Photon-based FLASH systems face engineering challenges in simultaneously achieving dose rates above 40 Gy/s and stereotactic beam characteristics, particularly heat management and multi-angle delivery.
Proton and heavy ion systems require further development in beam delivery and scanning speed to achieve FLASH-compatible stereotactic delivery.

Clinical translation requires specialized ultra-high dose rate dosimetry, quality assurance protocols, treatment planning systems optimizing spatial and temporal delivery, and new image guidance approaches.
42004842.reviewer_note: This is a technical/engineering review of platforms and requirements rather than an experimental or radiobiology study; the keyword-model category (Radiobiology) does not match the content, which centers on accelerator, dosimetry, and planning integration for stereotactic FLASH delivery. No new experimental data, dose values, or dose rates specific to a tested system are given, limiting ability to assess consistency with quantitative registered claims beyond general restatement (e.g., the >40 Gy/s threshold echoing BIO-002).
42004842.summary: This review surveys emerging FLASH radiotherapy platforms and technical requirements for combining ultra-high dose rate delivery with stereotactic radiosurgery and stereotactic body radiotherapy. It contrasts electron systems, which have supported preclinical FLASH work but have limited penetration for stereotactic use, with photon systems facing engineering barriers in heat management and multi-angle delivery at dose rates above 40 Gy/s, and proton/heavy ion systems that offer Bragg peak advantages but need further development in beam delivery and scanning speed. The paper discusses novel accelerator designs, beam monitoring systems, dosimetry for ultra-high dose rate measurement, quality assurance protocols, treatment planning systems addressing spatial and temporal optimization, and image guidance strategies. No specific preclinical or clinical dose, dose rate, or outcome data from a particular study are reported.

key_findings: OSLDs calibrated against a reference ion chamber provided dose reporting reproducible within ±5%, with precision improved by averaging multiple chips.
Scintillator-measured pulse-to-pulse stability agreed with diamond detector measurements within ±1%.
The diamond detector resolved intra-pulse stability and detected beam instabilities associated with poor beam tuning.
Combined use of OSLD, film, scintillator, and diamond detectors enabled redundant, time-resolved in-vivo dosimetry in a clinical UHDR trial setting, though resource-intensive.
42005725.reviewer_note: This paper addresses in-vivo detector performance and redundancy for clinical UHDR trials rather than reference dosimetry standardization per se; it does not directly test recombination correction (DOS-001) or attempt to establish a primary standard (DOS-002), so no contradiction is flagged, though the described reliance on ion-chamber calibration and multi-detector redundancy is consistent with the absence of an established primary UHDR standard noted in DOS-002.
42005725.summary: This study reports a multi-detector in-vivo dosimetry approach for a clinical UHDR trial delivered on a modified C-arm linac (9 MeV, dose per pulse 1.08 Gy, average dose rate 216 Gy/s). Four detector systems were evaluated: OSLDs and radiochromic film as passive detectors, and a scintillator and diamond detector as active, time-resolved systems, positioned via a 3D-printed mount or directly on patient skin. OSLDs calibrated against a reference ion chamber gave dose reporting reproducible within ±5%, improved by averaging multiple chips. Scintillator-measured pulse-to-pulse stability agreed with diamond detector measurements within ±1%, and the diamond detector additionally resolved intra-pulse stability, identifying beam instabilities from poor tuning.

key_findings: A brass collimator with 71 divergently-aligned 0.5 cm apertures enabled proton FLASH-SFRT delivery on a clinical synchrocyclotron.
Lynx PT scintillator dose-rate response was within ±1% between UHDR and conventional dose rate.
Experimental spot-trajectory profiles matched each other (>98.0% gamma pass) and TPS predictions (>95.6% gamma pass) at 2%/2mm criteria, with deviations beyond 4.5 cm off-axis.
Absolute dose measurements at peak and valley regions agreed with expectations within 1.32%±1.99% and -1.43%±3.15%.
Voxel-wise dose rates for targeted spot trajectories exceeded 60 Gy/s (mean) and 300 Gy/s (max) over central apertures.
42009045.reviewer_note: This is an engineering/dosimetric feasibility study for a spatially fractionated proton FLASH delivery system; it does not report biological endpoints or dose-rate thresholds for sparing, so it neither confirms nor contradicts BIO-001/BIO-002. The scintillator dose-rate-independence finding is consistent with but does not directly test DOS-001 (ionization chamber recombination), since ion chambers here were used only for cross-calibration at reference conditions.
42009045.summary: This study evaluates the feasibility of ultra-high-dose-rate proton spatially fractionated radiotherapy (FLASH-SFRT) on a compact IBA Proteus ONE synchrocyclotron using a custom 71-aperture brass collimator with 0.5 cm diameter apertures divergently matched to isocenter. Lynx PT scintillator, Razor Nano, and microDiamond detectors, cross-calibrated against an ADCL-calibrated PPC05 ion chamber, were used to measure 2D dose profiles and absolute doses at 2.0 cm solid-water depth for uniform and targeted spot trajectories. Lynx scintillator response at ultra-high dose rate agreed with conventional dose-rate response within ±1%, gamma pass rates (2%/2mm) between experimental spot trajectories exceeded 98.0%, and experiment-to-TPS comparisons exceeded 95.6%, with deviations appearing at off-axis distances beyond 4.5 cm. Absolute peak and valley dose measurements agreed with predictions within 1.32% ± 1.99% and -1.43% ± 3.15%, respectively. Pencil-beam-scanning voxel-wise maximum dose rates for targeted spot trajectories over the central nine apertures exceeded 60 Gy/s (mean) and 300 Gy/s (dose-averaged).

key_findings: Discrete ordinates Boltzmann dose calculation for a scanned 17.5 MeV electron beam agreed with radiochromic film measurements in water to within 3% experimental uncertainty at all depths.

In a six-patient retrospective planning comparison for superficial brain metastases, scanned electron beam plans yielded superior conformity index (1.02 ± 0.13) versus passively scattered proton UHDR (1.54 ± 0.13), proton arc, and robotic photon plans (1.35 ± 0.26), p < 0.05, with acceptable brain V12Gy and skin dose.
42009057.reviewer_note: This is a dose calculation and comparative treatment planning study rather than an accelerator or beam delivery engineering paper; the keyword-model category (Beam Delivery & Technology) undervalues the planning/optimization emphasis, so it was recategorized to Treatment Planning & Optimization. The paper does not engage with dose-rate metric definitions (PLAN-001) or biological/dosimetric claims, so no contradictions were identified; it is a physics/planning feasibility study without in vivo or dose-rate-effect endpoints.
42009057.summary: This study develops a beam model and discrete ordinates Boltzmann solver for treatment planning with a scanned 17.5 MeV quasi-monoenergetic electron beam from the PITZ facility at DESY-Zeuthen, intended for ultra-high dose rate delivery to superficial brain metastases. Beam profiles measured with radiochromic film in a water tank were used to build a Gaussian source model combined with CSDA-based electron transport, and the calculated dose distribution agreed with measurement to within 3% at all depths. Applied retrospectively to six patients, the scanned electron beam plans achieved a better conformity index than passively scattered proton (UHDR), proton arc, or robotic photon plans (1.02 ± 0.13 versus 1.54 ± 0.13 and 1.35 ± 0.26, median ± hemi-range, p < 0.05), with brain V12Gy and skin dose reported as acceptable across all modalities.

key_findings: 25 metabolites were consistently differentially regulated across 10 Gy, 12 Gy, and 14 Gy vs. 0 Gy photon FLASH-IR comparisons in mouse intestinal contents
3-hydroxyanthranilate showed a dose-dependent positive correlation with FLASH-IR dose
13 metabolites including guanosine, adenosine monophosphate, and hydroquinone showed negative correlation with increasing FLASH-IR dose
Enrichment analysis identified PI3K-AKT signaling, tyrosine metabolism, and purine metabolism as perturbed pathways
42011476.reviewer_note: Abstract does not report dose rate, pulse structure, or beam energy, and includes no conventional-dose-rate irradiation arm for comparison, so this study cannot be evaluated against BIO-001/BIO-002/BIO-003 dose-rate or sparing thresholds. It is a dose-response metabolomic characterization within FLASH-IR only, not a mechanism or hardware paper, hence retained under Radiobiology per the whole-animal tissue-endpoint criterion.
42011476.summary: C57BL/6J mice received 0, 10, 12, or 14 Gy of photon FLASH irradiation with no conventional-dose-rate comparison arm; the abstract does not report the dose rate used. Intestinal contents were collected 3.5 days post-irradiation and analyzed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry to characterize dose-dependent metabolic changes. Across the 10 Gy, 12 Gy, and 14 Gy vs. 0 Gy comparisons, 25 differential metabolites were consistently regulated, with 3-hydroxyanthranilate showing a positive dose correlation and 13 metabolites (including guanosine, adenosine monophosphate, and hydroquinone) showing negative correlation with increasing dose. Pathway enrichment implicated PI3K-AKT signaling, tyrosine metabolism, and purine metabolism as perturbed cascades following photon FLASH irradiation.

contradictions.explanation: The paper models plasmid DNA damage reduction via intertrack effects and oxygen/chemical competition rather than oxygen depletion magnitude in vivo, and finds the damage-reduction effect vanishes at cell-like scavenging capacities, which is consistent with but does not directly test the in vivo oxygen depletion insufficiency claim; it adds a mechanistic caveat about scavenging-capacity dependence rather than contradicting the claim outright.

key_findings: Model reproduced published conventional-dose-rate SSB yields across a range of scavenging capacities within 2% statistical uncertainty
At low scavenging capacities, ultra-high dose rate (2x10^7 Gy/s) versus conventional (0.1 Gy/s) produced 54.7% fewer SSBs and 73.5% fewer DSBs at 100 Gy from 225 kVp x-rays
At biologically relevant (cell-like) scavenging capacities, the dose-rate-dependent damage difference was within statistical uncertainty
No difference in WR-1065-mediated chemical repair was observed between UHDR and CONV
Reduction in DNA damage at low scavenging capacity attributed to intertrack effect rather than a mechanism expected to persist at cell-relevant scavenging capacities
42013902.reviewer_note: This is an in-silico plasmid DNA damage model, not an in vivo or cellular measurement, so it bears indirectly on MECH-001 (oxygen depletion) and BIO-002/BIO-001 (dose-rate and timing thresholds for tissue sparing) without directly testing those systems; flagged as qualifying rather than contradicting given the different endpoint (plasmid SSB/DSB yield) from the tissue-sparing claims.
42013902.summary: This study uses TOPAS-nBio track-structure Monte Carlo simulations to model radiation-induced damage to pUC19 plasmid DNA (50 microgram/ml) in oxygenated (21%) aqueous solution containing DMSO (0.01-100 mM), irradiated with 225 kVp x-rays to 100 Gy in a single pulse at conventional dose rate (0.1 Gy/s) versus ultra-high dose rate (2x10^7 Gy/s). Two models were tested: one without DNA repair and one incorporating chemical repair via WR-1065 competing with oxygen. At conventional dose rate the model reproduced published single-strand break yields across scavenging capacities within 2% statistical uncertainty. At low scavenging capacities, ultra-high dose rate irradiation produced a 54.7% reduction in single-strand breaks and a 73.5% reduction in double-strand breaks compared to conventional dose rate, but at biologically relevant scavenging capacities this difference fell within statistical uncertainty, and no difference in WR-1065-mediated chemical repair was observed between dose rates. The authors attribute the dose-rate-dependent damage reduction seen experimentally at low DNA concentration and low scavenging capacity to an intertrack effect, predicting no such reduction at cell-like scavenging capacities.

key_findings: Three tomographic reconstruction algorithms (FBAI, FBP, MLEM) reproduced global depth-dose behavior when validated against Monte Carlo ground-truth simulations.

Experimental RLI-based dose reconstructions from a plastic scintillator cube agreed with Gafchromic film dosimetry across UHDR (9 MeV FLASH electron linac) and conventional dose-rate conditions (6 MeV electron linac, 6 MeV photon CyberKnife), with gamma values predominantly below unity.

The technique reproduced depth-dose profiles across different field sizes and dose rates, supporting its use as a complementary real-time, spatially resolved dosimetry tool for UHDR beam monitoring and quality assurance.
42026122.reviewer_note: No numeric dose, dose-rate, or gamma pass-rate values are given in the abstract, limiting quantitative reporting in the summary. This work introduces a new relative dosimetry/imaging technique rather than addressing ionization chamber recombination correction (DOS-001) or primary standards (DOS-002) directly; it could be considered a contribution to the broader UHDR dosimetry landscape referenced by DOS-002 but does not itself report cross-institutional comparison data, so it is not flagged as a contradiction.
42026122.summary: This study develops a proof-of-concept method for three-dimensional dose reconstruction from radioluminescence imaging (RLI) of a plastic scintillator cube, using cylindrical beam symmetry and inverse tomographic reconstruction algorithms (Fourier-based Abel inversion, filtered back-projection, and maximum-likelihood expectation maximization). The methods were first benchmarked against Monte Carlo ground-truth dose distributions, then validated experimentally under ultra-high-dose-rate conditions using a 9 MeV FLASH electron linac and under conventional dose-rate conditions using a 6 MeV electron linac and a 6 MeV photon CyberKnife system. Reconstructed dose distributions were compared to Gafchromic film measurements via gamma index analysis and depth-dose profiles, with gamma values predominantly below unity and reconstructed profiles closely matching film-based reference measurements across dose rates and field sizes. The authors conclude that RLI-based 3D dose reconstruction is experimentally simple and applicable to both conventional and FLASH radiotherapy dosimetry and beam monitoring.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports that radiolytic oxygen depletion (gO2) correlates with baseline pO2 and with the presence or absence of toxicity sparing at ultra-high dose rate, suggesting oxygen depletion plays a mechanistic role that modulates sparing in this model, which qualifies the claim that oxygen depletion alone is insufficient to account for sparing rather than directly contradicting it, since sparing was absent at both very low and very high pO2 extremes.

The paper finds that sparing depends on baseline tissue pO2 rather than dose rate threshold alone, showing no sparing under anoxia or carbogen-induced hyperoxia despite dose rates within the sparing range, indicating that mean dose rate above ~40 Gy/s is not sufficient by itself to guarantee sparing and that tissue oxygenation is an additional modulating variable.

key_findings: Skin sparing at ultra-high dose rate (~240 Gy/s) versus conventional dose rate (~0.16 Gy/s) at 25 Gy occurred in cohorts with moderate baseline pO2 (partial clamping ~7 mmHg, room air ~12 mmHg, 100% oxygen ~16 mmHg), with significant reduction in ulceration progression only in the room air cohort.
No sparing effect was observed under complete anoxia (pO2 ~0 mmHg) or under carbogen-induced hyperoxia (pO2 ~21 mmHg), the latter holding across a dose range of 15-25 Gy.
In vivo radiolytic oxygen consumption (gO2) correlated with initial pO2 under ultra-high dose rate conditions across pO2 ~4-16 mmHg, with ulceration predominantly occurring above 16 mmHg.
At 25 Gy, anoxic tissue showed low toxicity scores (<1) with no difference between ultra-high and conventional dose rate.
42030995.reviewer_note: This study focuses on a specific normal-tissue (skin) endpoint and oxygen modulation rather than tumor control, dosimetry standards, or dose-rate metric definitions, so most registered claims outside MECH-001 and BIO-002 are not directly addressed.
42030995.summary: This study used murine leg skin irradiated with a FLASH Mobetron 9 MeV linac at 25 Gy, comparing ultra-high dose rate (approximately 240 Gy/s) to conventional dose rate (approximately 0.16 Gy/s), while systematically varying baseline tissue pO2 across five cohorts using inhaled room air, 100% oxygen, carbogen, and partial or full vascular occlusion. Skin sparing at ultra-high dose rate was observed with partial clamping (pO2 approximately 7 mmHg), room air (approximately 12 mmHg), and 100% oxygen (approximately 16 mmHg), with significant reduction in ulceration progression only in the room air group. No sparing effect was seen under complete anoxia (pO2 approximately 0 mmHg) or under carbogen-induced hyperoxia (pO2 approximately 21 mmHg), and this held across doses from 15 to 25 Gy under carbogen. Radiolytic oxygen consumption (gO2) correlated with initial pO2 under ultra-high dose rate conditions across a pO2 range of approximately 4-16 mmHg, with ulceration occurring predominantly above 16 mmHg. At 25 Gy, toxicity scores under anoxia were low (<1) and did not differ between dose rates.

key_findings: Single-fraction FLASH RT (17 Gy) reduced lung and heart fibrosis versus CONV RT at 28 weeks post-irradiation (P<.0001).
FLASH RT reduced circulating lymphocyte apoptosis and accelerated recovery of CD4+, CD8+, CD3+, NK, and B cell populations in both single-fraction and multifraction (2 Gy x 5) regimens.
CONV RT produced sustained increases in regulatory T cells and PD-1/PD-L1 expression on T- and B-cells at 2 and 5 months post-irradiation, not seen with FLASH RT.
CONV RT sustained Chk1-STAT3 pathway activation in splenic CD45+ immune cells, correlating with increased PD-1/PD-L1 expression.
42031222.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report a specific dose rate value (Gy/s) for the FLASH arm, only the platform (Mobetron), so this study cannot be checked against BIO-002's quantitative dose-rate threshold. No tumor control endpoint is reported, so BIO-003 is not addressed by this paper. The mechanistic Chk1-STAT3 signaling analysis is based on measured immunofluorescence/Western blot data from an in vivo model rather than a computational model, supporting Radiobiology over Modeling & Mechanisms.
42031222.summary: This study compares thoracic FLASH RT and conventional dose rate RT (CONV RT) in C57BL/6 mice using electron beams delivered by the Mobetron, testing single-fraction (17 Gy) and multifraction (2 Gy x 5) regimens. FLASH RT significantly reduced lung and heart fibrosis at 28 weeks post-irradiation compared to CONV RT (P<.0001) and produced reduced circulating lymphocyte apoptosis with accelerated recovery of CD4+, CD8+, CD3+, NK, and B cell populations in both fractionation schemes. CONV RT induced long-lasting increases in regulatory T cells and sustained PD-1/PD-L1 expression on T- and B-cells at 2 and 5 months post-irradiation. Mechanistic analysis of splenic CD45+ immune cells showed CONV RT sustained activation of the Chk1-STAT3 pathway, correlating with elevated PD-1/PD-L1 expression, whereas FLASH RT reduced activation of this axis.

key_findings: A start-to-end simulation chain links particle-in-cell laser-plasma acceleration, beamline transport (quadrupoles, collimator, dipoles), and GEANT4 dose deposition modeling for VHEE radiotherapy.

Polychromatic VHEE beams generated from laser-plasma acceleration, after collimation and arrangement into a beam array, produce dose distributions capable of reaching deep regions in water and heterogeneous bone-insert phantoms.
Multifield irradiation from multiple incidence angles is simulated to demonstrate multi-angle conformal delivery at the isocenter.
42031987.reviewer_note: Abstract does not report dose rate, absolute dose values, or biological/tumor endpoints, so no direct comparison to registered dosimetry or radiobiology claims is possible. This is a pure simulation/feasibility study of beam delivery and dose deposition, not an experimental dosimetry or radiobiology paper, so it does not engage with DOS or BIO claims despite topical overlap with VHEE beam delivery.
42031987.summary: This study presents a start-to-end simulation workflow for very high-energy electron (VHEE) radiotherapy driven by a laser-plasma accelerator, using parameters of the OONA laser (less than 1.3 J, less than 25 fs pulse duration) at the Weizmann Institute of Science. Particle-in-cell simulations generate realistic polychromatic electron beams, which are then transported through a beamline of quadrupoles, a collimator, and dipoles to form a beam array, with GEANT4 used to compute dose deposition in water and heterogeneous bone-insert phantoms. Multifield irradiation from multiple incidence angles is modeled to simulate multi-angle conformal delivery at the isocenter. The workflow demonstrates that polychromatic VHEE beams delivered through this beamline configuration can achieve dose distributions favorable for reaching deep-seated targets within the phantom.

key_findings: Fiber-tip SMOUT probe (400 μm diameter) fabricated and optically/acoustically characterized: ORW ~773 nm, acoustic central frequency ~300 kHz, -6 dB bandwidth ~160 kHz
Single-pulse noise equivalent dose ~5.19 cGy, reported as independent of dose rate
Probe causes negligible perturbation to FLASH electron beam transmittance
1-D scanning of the probe enabled 2-D dose distribution mapping with high consistency to reference dosimetry
42037989.reviewer_note: This is a detector/sensor development paper for acoustic dosimetry (iRAI) under UHDR electron beam, fitting Physics & Dosimetry per the taxonomy's detector-response and relative-dosimetry criteria. It does not perform a cross-institutional intercomparison or address primary-standard status, so it neither confirms nor contradicts DOS-002; it simply introduces a new candidate detection modality. No dose rate range, tumor/tissue endpoint, or biological outcome is reported, so no linkage to BIO or MECH claims is applicable.
42037989.summary: This paper reports the design, fabrication, and characterization of a fiber-tip surface-micromachined optical ultrasound transducer (SMOUT) probe, 400 μm in diameter, intended for ionizing radiation acoustic imaging (iRAI) during UHDR electron beam delivery. The probe exhibits an optical resonance wavelength of approximately 773 nm, an acoustic central frequency of approximately 300 kHz, a -6 dB acoustic bandwidth of approximately 160 kHz, and a single-pulse noise equivalent dose of approximately 5.19 cGy that is reported as dose-rate independent. The authors report negligible disturbance of the probe to FLASH electron beam irradiation and demonstrate 2-D dose distribution mapping via 1-D scanning with high consistency relative to reference measurement. The work targets acoustic-based online dosimetry as an alternative to piezoelectric sensors, which the authors note suffer from electronic noise and neutron damage under UHDR conditions.

key_findings: Brass apertures reduced lateral penumbra at entrance, midpoint, and Bragg peak positions in single-energy Bragg peak proton FLASH plans, with the reduction increasing with greater range shifter pullback distance (10, 20, 30 cm) and being larger for 5 cm fields than 3 cm fields.
In an rGBM plan, apertures improved GTV dose conformity and reduced OAR dose but decreased ultra-high dose-rate (V40Gy(RBE)/s) coverage for both GTV and OARs.
Ultra-high dose-rate coverage of the GTV was unaffected by dose threshold choice (0, 2, 5 Gy), whereas brain ultra-high dose-rate coverage increased with increasing dose threshold.
42050792.reviewer_note: This paper is a treatment-planning and dose-rate-metric study for proton SEBP FLASH delivery, evaluating a planning/hardware trade-off (apertures vs. penumbra and dose-rate coverage) rather than a pure detector/dosimetry measurement study; it is more aligned with Treatment Planning & Optimization (PLAN-001 context on dose-rate metric definitions) than the keyword-suggested Physics & Dosimetry, though it also touches beam delivery hardware (apertures, range shifters). No direct contradiction of registered claims is reported; findings on dose-rate/conformity trade-offs are consistent with existing planning-metric ambiguity (PLAN-001) but do not alter its substance.
42050792.summary: This study evaluates brass apertures in proton pencil beam scanning single-energy Bragg peak FLASH radiotherapy plans, using an in-house planning system with MCSquare Monte Carlo simulation for dose and dose-rate calculation. Aperture effects on lateral penumbra were assessed in water phantoms for 3 and 5 cm square fields under varying universal range shifter pullback (10, 20, 30 cm) and air gap (5, 10, 15 cm) conditions, and in a recurrent glioblastoma (rGBM) clinical plan using dose thresholds of 0, 2, and 5 Gy for the ultra-high dose-rate metric V40Gy(RBE)/s. Apertures significantly reduced lateral penumbra across entrance, midpoint, and Bragg peak positions, with greater reduction for larger pullback distances and for the 5 cm field compared to the 3 cm field. In the rGBM case, apertures improved gross tumor volume dose conformity and reduced organ-at-risk dose but decreased ultra-high dose-rate coverage for both GTV and OARs, while maintaining the FLASH ratio in high-dose regions.

contradictions.explanation: The study confirms isoeffective tumour control between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT at matched physical dose across single and fractionated regimens in TNBC models, consistent with BIO-003, but qualifies it by showing that this isoeffectiveness at the growth-delay and immune-infiltration level coexists with distinct underlying immunotranscriptomic programs, indicating that iso-efficacy in tumour control does not imply mechanistic equivalence.

key_findings: Tumour growth delay was iso-efficacy between FLASH-RT (5-5.79x10^6 Gy/s) and CONV-RT (0.2 Gy/s) across single-dose (14 or 20 Gy) and fractionated (5x5.2 Gy, 10x3 Gy) regimens in 4T1 and MDA-MB-231 TNBC models.
No differences in immune cell infiltration were detected between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT by histology and flow cytometry.

RNA sequencing at 24 h post-irradiation showed FLASH-RT preserved chemokine (CXCL9/10/11, NES = 2.516) and interferon alpha/gamma signalling (NES = 2.998, 3.235) that CONV-RT downregulated, alongside conserved expression of negative regulators of interferon and inflammatory signalling (PD-L1, IL18BP).
42061755.reviewer_note: Study does not address normal-tissue sparing, oxygen depletion, dosimetry, or dose-rate thresholds, so BIO-001, BIO-002, MECH-001, DOS-001/002, CLIN-001, and PLAN-001 are not addressed and not contradicted, merely outside scope.
42061755.summary: Using subcutaneous and orthotopic 4T1 and MDA-MB-231 murine triple-negative breast cancer models in female BALB/c or Swiss nude mice, this study compared FLASH-RT (5-5.79x10^6 Gy/s) to CONV-RT (0.2 Gy/s) delivered as single doses (14 or 20 Gy) or fractionated regimens (5x5.2 Gy or 10x3 Gy). Tumour growth delay was iso-efficacy between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT across all regimens, and histology and flow cytometry showed no differences in immune cell infiltration. Bulk RNA sequencing of 4T1 tumours at 24 h, 5 days, and 2 weeks post-irradiation revealed that FLASH-RT preserved chemokine expression (NES = 2.516, including CXCL9, 10, 11) and interferon alpha/gamma signalling via ISGF3 (NES = 2.998 and 3.235 respectively) at 24 h, which CONV-RT downregulated. FLASH-RT also conserved expression of negative regulators of type I/II interferon (NES = 2.108 and 1.784) and of inflammation (NES = 1.88, including PD-L1 and IL18BP), proposed to explain the discordance between transcriptomic divergence and unchanged immune infiltration.

key_findings: Respiratory gating latency on a Varian Trilogy linac was measured as normally distributed, with mean/SD of 2.0±0.8, 2.1±2.8, and 2.4±1.9 ms for beam-on and 1.3±0.9, 1.9±2.9, and 1.8±2.1 ms for beam-off at 60, 90, and 180 Hz respectively.
An adaptive pulse-delivery method (using only delivered-pulse signal) achieved >99% success at 90 Hz and 95% at 180 Hz.
A synchronization method (additionally using internal pulse-timing signal) achieved >99% success at 90 Hz but only 80% at 180 Hz.
The methods enabled generation of custom pulse sequences not natively available on the clinical linac platform.
42094274.reviewer_note: This paper does not report a biological endpoint, dose, or dose rate value, and therefore cannot be checked against BIO-001/BIO-002/BIO-003 timing claims despite conceptual relevance to precise pulse-timing control needed for such experiments. It is an engineering/instrumentation study on pulse-count delivery accuracy using a clinical linac's built-in monitor chamber and respiratory gating hardware, consistent with the Beam Delivery & Technology category.
42094274.summary: This work addresses respiratory gating latency on a Varian Trilogy clinical linear accelerator used for preclinical electron FLASH irradiation, characterizing beam-on/beam-off timing errors at 60, 90, and 180 Hz pulse repetition frequencies using custom controller boards and relay circuitry. Mean latencies were 2.0±0.8 ms (60 Hz), 2.1±2.8 ms (90 Hz), and 2.4±1.9 ms (180 Hz) for beam-on, and 1.3±0.9 ms, 1.9±2.9 ms, and 1.8±2.1 ms respectively for beam-off, with similar values across beam-on and beam-off and across frequencies. Two correction methods (adaptive, using only delivered-pulse signal, and synchronization, additionally using internal pulse-timing signal) achieved successful pulse-number delivery exceeding 99% at 90 Hz, and 95% (adaptive) versus 80% (synchronization) at 180 Hz. The authors report that accounting for latency enables reliable delivery of specified pulse counts, including custom pulse sequences not natively supported by the system, for single-fraction and fractionated preclinical dosing regimens. No biological endpoint, dose, or dose-rate value is reported in the abstract; the study is purely instrumentation/engineering focused on pulse-count delivery accuracy.

key_findings: Significant cell killing at 48 h post-irradiation for doses >=10 Gy delivered at UHDR (40 Gy/s) versus low dose rate (0.5-5 Gy/min) in HEM/MM96L and CCD841/CaCo2 cell pairs.
MM96L melanoma cells were ~10% less resistant to UHDR than HEM cells; a similar differential was observed between CCD841 and CaCo2 cells.
Under hypoxia, HEM cells showed minimal viability loss at >=10 Gy UHDR whereas MM96L cells showed significant cell loss under the same conditions.
Gold nanoparticle pretreatment (1 mM) in MM96L cells produced 50% dose enhancement at 10 Gy UHDR versus 15% at low dose rate.
42095785.reviewer_note: This is an in vitro synchrotron X-ray study without whole-animal tumor/tissue endpoints, so it does not directly test BIO-002 (in vivo dose rate threshold) or BIO-003 (tumour control isoeffectiveness), though its differential cell killing results between normal and tumor-derived lines are thematically related. The hypoxia results relate to MECH-001 but examine cell viability rather than in vivo tissue sparing, so no direct contradiction is claimed. Dose rate of 40 Gy/s is stated as the UHDR condition but pulse structure/temporal delivery details are not given, limiting assessment against BIO-001.
42095785.summary: This in vitro study exposed human epidermal melanocytes (HEM), MM96L melanoma cells, CCD841 colon epithelial cells, and CaCo2 colorectal adenocarcinoma cells to synchrotron-based X-ray beams delivered at low dose rate (0.5-5 Gy/min) or ultra-high dose rate (40 Gy/s) to assess a FLASH effect. At doses of 10 Gy or greater delivered at UHDR, significant cell killing was observed at 48 hours post-irradiation compared with low dose rate exposure in both cell groupings, with MM96L melanoma cells approximately 10% less resistant to UHDR than HEM cells and a similar differential seen between CCD841 and CaCo2 cells. Under hypoxic conditions, HEM cells showed minimal loss of viability at 10 Gy or greater UHDR while hypoxic MM96L cells showed significant cell loss. Pretreatment of MM96L cells with 1 mM gold nanoparticles followed by 10 Gy UHDR X-rays produced 50% dose enhancement, compared with 15% dose enhancement observed at low dose rate.

contradictions.explanation: The paper directly demonstrates that FLASH effect quantification is highly sensitive to the choice of dose-rate model (FEM vs ADR) and to scanning parameters, reinforcing the registered claim that no consensus dose-rate definition exists and that formulations are not interchangeable, with concrete magnitude differences shown between models.

key_findings: FLASH effect metrics in CTV and skin are highly sensitive to vertical scan speed (10-20 mm/ms) and to choice of dose-rate model (FEM vs ADR), with substantially different magnitudes reported by each model.
Split-field delivery increased temporal distance between scanning columns, improving FLASH effect and reducing FLASH-corrected CTV mean dose by up to 9.2 Gy (ADR model).

Genetic-algorithm-based spot path optimization shortened scan time and achieved FLASH effect comparable to split-field delivery, with CTV mean dose reduction of 7.87 Gy and skin mean dose reductions of 2 to 3 Gy.
42107782.reviewer_note: This is a treatment planning and dose-rate modeling study for proton transmission FLASH delivery, not a cellular, molecular, or animal radiobiology study; the keyword-model category of Radiobiology appears mismatched. No new in vivo or in vitro biological endpoint data are reported, so no direct contradiction of BIO-001, BIO-002, or BIO-003 claims arises, only a methodological illustration of PLAN-001's model-dependence concern.
42107782.summary: This retrospective planning study modeled proton transmission FLASH radiotherapy for postmastectomy chest wall treatment (32 Gy in 5 fractions) in five left-sided breast cancer patients using single-energy (249 MeV) tangential transmission beams with a supplemental en face beam. FLASH effect was quantified using two dose-rate models, Krieger's FLASH effectiveness model (FEM) and Folkerts' average dose-rate (ADR) framework, applying a voxel threshold of at least 4 Gy at at least 40 Gy/s and a dose adjustment factor of 0.67. Increasing vertical scan speed from 10 to 20 mm/ms increased FLASH effect in the clinical target volume by 22% (ADR) and 12% (FEM), and in skin from 41.4% to 58.8% (ADR) and 8.4% to 13.1% (FEM). Split-field delivery and genetic-algorithm-optimized spot sequencing improved temporal separation between scan columns, yielding up to 9.2 Gy and 7.87 Gy reductions respectively in FLASH-corrected CTV mean dose under the ADR model, with skin mean dose reductions of 2 to 3 Gy.

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states bulk radiolytic oxygen depletion alone is insufficient to explain in vivo sparing magnitude. This paper does not dispute that bulk-tissue depletion is insufficient but reframes the mechanism at the DNA-target level within niche microenvironments, proposing that sparing depends on baseline nuclear oxygenation falling in an intermediate physiologic-hypoxia window rather than on bulk oxygen depletion magnitude alone, offering a refined mechanistic account rather than a direct contradiction.

key_findings: A modified LPL model with an explicit Precursor Lesion population and oxygen-dependent fixation kinetics reproduces oxygen-mediated FLASH-sparing trends without prescribing dose-rate-dependent radiosensitivity.
Sparing is predicted to be largest at an intermediate baseline nuclear oxygen tension (pO2,0 = 3 mmHg) corresponding to the steep, oxygen-responsive region of the OER curve.
Sparing is predicted to be minimal at either extreme of baseline oxygenation, near the OER floor (0.2 mmHg) or the OER saturation plateau (30 mmHg).

The framework distinguishes bulk vascular oxygenation from an effective DNA target-level oxygenation to reconcile oxygen-depletion arguments with clinically relevant fraction sizes (the 'oxygen paradox').
42108222.reviewer_note: This is a theoretical/computational model paper with no reported experimental dose, dose rate, or beam quality; it does not measure a FLASH sparing effect but predicts conditions under which the effect should be largest. It should be distinguished in the corpus from experimental radiobiology studies reporting measured sparing at specific dose rates.
42108222.summary: This paper presents a mechanistic extension of the classical Lethal and Potentially Lethal (LPL) model that introduces an explicit Precursor Lesion population whose fixation into lethal or potentially lethal damage depends on a time-varying nuclear oxygen tension. The model couples radiolytic oxygen depletion and reduced-order reoxygenation kinetics to a mechanistic exponential OER formulation, distinguishing bulk vascular oxygenation from a lower effective DNA target-level oxygenation in stem-cell niches. No specific beam quality, dose, or dose rate values for a physical irradiation are given; the study is purely computational. In the reference parameter set, oxygen-mediated sparing under ultra-high dose rate delivery is largest when baseline nuclear pO2 is 3 mmHg, an intermediate physiologic-hypoxia regime on the steep portion of the OER curve, and is minimal at pO2 of 0.2 mmHg (OER floor) or 30 mmHg (OER saturation plateau). Sensitivity analyses shift the magnitude and threshold of the effect but preserve the intermediate oxygen window.

key_findings: Silicon photomultiplier saturation correction reached a multiplier of up to 55% across the four ZnSe:O probes
Depth-dependent scintillator under-response (quenching) reached up to 12% at the distal SOBP edge
Calibrated system achieved positional stability within ±0.1 mm and dose agreement within 0.5% versus ionisation chamber reference across a range of UHDR beam currents in the SOBP
Beam spot FWHM broadened from 8.3 mm at shallow depth to 21.5 mm near range end, with profiles fit by two Gaussian cores plus a Lorentzian tail
Maximum instantaneous dose rate decreased from 800 Gy/s in the entrance plateau to 280 Gy/s in the SOBP
42108226.reviewer_note: This paper concerns scintillator detector calibration for proton SOBP time-resolved dosimetry and does not report on ionization chamber recombination correction methodology (DOS-001) or cross-institutional intercomparisons (DOS-002); it develops a single-institution calibration approach for a different detector modality and does not test biological, mechanistic, or planning claims in the registry, so no direct contradiction, qualification, or supersession is identified.
42108226.summary: This study calibrates a fibre-coupled ZnSe:O scintillator detector system, read out via silicon photomultipliers at 50 kHz, for time-resolved point dosimetry in the spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) of a clinical pencil-beam-scanning proton FLASH beam line, using a 5 cm SOBP generated by a 2D range modulator from a mono-energetic beam. The calibration addresses silicon photomultiplier saturation (up to 55% multiplier) and depth-dependent scintillator under-response/quenching (up to 12% at the distal SOBP edge), with an ionisation chamber serving as reference dosimeter. Validation across a range of UHDR beam currents showed positional stability within ±0.1 mm and dose agreement within 0.5% of reference values for all four probes. Beam characterisation using the calibrated system showed spot FWHM broadening from 8.3 mm at shallow depth to 21.5 mm near range end, with profiles composed of two Gaussian cores and a Lorentzian tail, and maximum instantaneous dose rate falling from 800 Gy/s in the entrance plateau to 280 Gy/s in the SOBP.

42109677.reviewer_note: This is a correction/erratum notice with no abstract content describing methods, dose, dose rate, or findings. Cannot assess scientific claims or contradictions without access to the original article's substantive content. Category assignment (Physics & Dosimetry) is based solely on the title's mention of dosimetry/calorimetry, consistent with the keyword-model suggestion, but confidence is low given the absence of any actual scientific findings to evaluate.
42109677.summary: This is a correction notice for a previously published article on range quality assurance measurements using a range calorimeter for clinical and FLASH proton beam therapy. The abstract contains no substantive scientific content beyond referencing the original article's DOI. No experimental details, dose rates, beam quality parameters, or findings are provided in this correction notice.

contradictions.explanation: The paper's finding that oxygen depletion alone cannot account for the sparing effect, but must act synergistically with radical recombination, is consistent with and refines MECH-001 rather than contradicting it; it adds a specific mechanistic pathway (radical recombination via long-lived secondary species) to the existing claim that oxygen depletion alone is insufficient.

key_findings: RMLE model reproduces in vitro prostate cancer cell survival dose-response curves under FLASH and conventional dose rates, in both normoxic and hypoxic conditions, and corrects high-dose overestimation seen with the standard LQ model.
The FLASH sparing effect observed is more pronounced under hypoxic conditions and cannot be explained by oxygen depletion alone.

A hierarchical regression decoupling radical survival probability (Ps) and oxygen-dependent damage fixation probability (Px) supports a synergistic mechanism combining radical recombination and oxygen depletion.

Track-track interaction simulations indicate that physical recombination sufficient to explain sparing at 600 Gy/s requires microsecond-scale interaction times (~10-100 microseconds), suggesting mediation by long-lived secondary chemical species rather than direct track overlap alone.
42119592.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify beam quality, modality, or absolute dose values used in the in vitro validation beyond the 600 Gy/s dose rate cited for track-structure simulations; these details would strengthen categorization confidence.
42119592.summary: This study develops the radical-mediated linear-exponential (RMLE) model, a mathematical extension of the linear-quadratic model that incorporates dose-rate dependent radical survival probability and oxygen-dependent damage fixation probability to describe cell survival under ultra-high dose rate conditions. The model was validated against in vitro prostate cancer cell survival data comparing FLASH and conventional dose rates under normoxic and hypoxic oxygenation. The RMLE model reproduced dose-response curves across all tested conditions and resolved a high-dose overestimation problem present in the standard LQ model. Analysis indicated that the sparing effect, more pronounced under hypoxia, could not be explained by oxygen depletion alone but instead required a synergistic interaction between radical recombination and oxygen depletion. Track-track interaction simulations further indicated that achieving the physical recombination needed at 600 Gy/s requires a microsecond-scale interaction time (tau ~10-100 microseconds), implicating long-lived secondary chemical species.

key_findings: Addition of a repurposed steering magnet enabled true 2D pencil beam scanning on Gantry 1, previously limited to fixed-beam or 1D delivery.
Software optimization of control processes and magnet settling times minimized inter-spot dead times, supporting local average dose rates up to 75 Gy/s over 100x24 mm2 fields.

A 1 kHz logging system permits reconstruction of lateral dose and dose-rate maps, validated against CCD (90% isodose contour) and micro-Diamond detector measurements across gantry angles from 0 to -120 degrees.
42128001.reviewer_note: This paper is primarily an engineering/hardware retrofit report (scanning magnet integration, control system, logging system) with dosimetric validation as a supporting element, so it is classified as Beam Delivery & Technology rather than the keyword-suggested Physics & Dosimetry. It does not engage with primary-standard or cross-institutional dosimetry questions (DOS-002) since it describes a single-institution system validation, so no contradiction is flagged; it is simply a different scope.
42128001.summary: This work describes hardware and control-system modifications to PSI Gantry 1, a proton pencil beam scanning unit, to enable true two-dimensional ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) scanning for FLASH research. A second (vertical) scanning direction was added by repurposing an existing steering magnet, inter-spot dead times were minimized via software synchronization of control processes and magnet settling times, and a 1 kHz logging system was introduced to reconstruct lateral dose and dose-rate distributions from recorded beam parameters. The system was commissioned for small fields (100x24 mm2) at gantry angles from 0 degrees to -120 degrees, achieving dose-uniform deliveries at local average dose rates up to 75 Gy/s. Reconstructed lateral dose distributions agreed with CCD measurements on the 90% isodose contour, and reconstructed dose-rate distributions were validated against micro-Diamond detector measurements.

key_findings: 2.5 cm wall thickness PLA applicator minimized out-of-field dose; 12.5 cm length optimized instantaneous dose rate and lateral flatness for 6 MeV and 9 MeV UHDR electron beams
Ultra-thin conductive Kapton shielding for the BCT caused <0.15% loss in beam energy fluence
MC-predicted doses (scaled via calibrated BCT) agreed with radiochromic film measurements to within 0.16%-1.68% across energies and field sizes in a tumor spheroid microchip phantom
42128006.reviewer_note: This paper presents a calibrated, applicator-integrated real-time dosimetry system (BCT) validated against film, but does not perform a cross-institutional intercomparison or address ionization chamber recombination correction directly, so it neither confirms nor contradicts DOS-001 or DOS-002; it may be relevant contextually as an example of instrument-level dosimetric development toward addressing the standardization gap noted in DOS-002, but this is not stated in the abstract.
42128006.summary: The study reports design and validation of a 3D-printed polylactic acid applicator (2.5 cm wall thickness, 12.5 cm length) integrating an electrostatically shielded beam current transformer (BCT) for real-time dose tracking during UHDR electron delivery on a Mobetron at 6 MeV and 9 MeV. Monte Carlo simulations (BEAMnrc, DOSRZnrc) guided applicator geometry to suppress out-of-field scatter and balance instantaneous dose rate against lateral dose uniformity, while ultra-thin conductive Kapton was selected as BCT shielding material, producing less than 0.15% loss in beam energy fluence. Validation in a microchip phantom for tumor spheroid culture compared MC-predicted, BCT-scaled doses against radiochromic film measurements, yielding agreement within 0.16%-1.68% depending on energy and field size. The work presents an applicator-integrated real-time dosimetry system intended for preclinical UHDR studies with flexible switching between FLASH and conventional dose-rate modes.

key_findings: Software-based service-mode reconfiguration switches a clinical TrueBeam between UHDR and conventional electron modes without accessing linac interior hardware
UHDR electron energies (9.2, 12.6 MeV) closely matched conventional beam energies (8.4, 11.7 MeV) with comparable depth-dose and profile characteristics
Dose per pulse up to 1.5 Gy/pulse (in vivo, 64 cm SSD) and 0.7 Gy/pulse (in vitro, 82 cm SSD) achieved with field flatness/symmetry maintained
Day-to-day output variation averaged <3% CV for UHDR and <1% CV for conventional mode
42155735.reviewer_note: This paper is primarily an engineering/feasibility demonstration of a reversible UHDR configuration method on existing clinical hardware, better matching Beam Delivery & Technology than the keyword-suggested Physics & Dosimetry, though it includes substantial dosimetric characterization (film, ion chamber, output reproducibility). No mean dose rate in Gy/s is reported, only dose-per-pulse values, limiting comparison to BIO-002. No recombination correction methodology or primary standard claims are addressed, so DOS-001/DOS-002 are neither supported nor contradicted.
42155735.summary: This work describes a reversible, noninvasive configuration of a clinical TrueBeam linac for ultra-high-dose-rate (UHDR) electron delivery, using built-in service mode software to retract the photon target and monitor chambers and load an unused electron scattering foil, with an external AC current transformer and downstream ionization chamber added for beam monitoring. UHDR electron energies of 9.2 and 12.6 MeV matched conventional-mode energies of 8.4 and 11.7 MeV, with percent depth-dose profiles agreeing through mouse- and cell-culture-relevant thicknesses. Maximum dose per pulse reached 1.5 Gy/pulse at 64 cm SSD (in vivo setup) and 0.7 Gy/pulse at 82 cm SSD (in vitro setup, up to 5x5 cm2 field), with field flatness and symmetry preserved between UHDR and conventional modes. Day-to-day output coefficients of variation averaged under 3% for UHDR and under 1% for conventional delivery.

key_findings: FLASH irradiation produced a dose-modifying factor of ~1.5 for skin toxicity after both single-dose and fractionated hemithorax irradiation in mice, compared with conventional dose-rate irradiation (P < .001).
FLASH-irradiated skin showed dampened immune activation and greater preservation of immune cell populations relative to conventionally irradiated skin.

CD8+ T-cell depletion exacerbated skin toxicity and inflammatory response after conventional irradiation but had no such effect after FLASH irradiation, indicating an immune-mediated component of FLASH-associated normal-tissue sparing.
The skin-sparing effect of FLASH was maintained under hypofractionated regimens and under immunocompromised conditions (CD8+ depletion).
42176866.reviewer_note: Abstract omits beam quality, specific dose values, and dose rate, so the paper cannot be checked against BIO-002 (dose-rate threshold) or BIO-001 (delivery-time threshold) claims. The immune-mediated mechanism proposed here (CD8+ T-cell dependence) is a mechanistic contribution distinct from oxygen depletion (MECH-001) and does not directly contradict it, but could be relevant as a complementary explanatory pathway for normal-tissue sparing; consider whether the wiki should register a new mechanistic claim around immune modulation. No tumor-control endpoint is reported, so BIO-003 is not addressed by this study.
42176866.summary: This study uses a mouse hemithorax irradiation model to quantify skin-sparing effects of FLASH radiation therapy delivered as single-dose and fractionated regimens, though the abstract does not specify beam quality, exact dose values, or dose rate. FLASH irradiation delayed onset and reduced severity of skin toxicity relative to conventional dose-rate irradiation (P < .001), with a dose-modifying factor of approximately 1.5 for both single and fractionated delivery. Multiplex gene expression and immune profiling showed dampened immune activation and greater preservation of immune cell populations in FLASH-irradiated skin. CD8+ T-cell depletion worsened skin toxicity and inflammatory response after conventional irradiation but not after FLASH irradiation, implicating CD8+ T-cell-dependent immune dysfunction in conventional-dose-rate toxicity.

contradictions.explanation: The paper delivered FLASH-PT at 268 Gy/s, well above the ~40-100 Gy/s range associated with sparing in BIO-002, yet found no FLASH-related sparing effect for microglia activation in brain tissue, indicating that dose-rate-dependent sparing may be endpoint- and tissue-specific rather than universally observed above threshold dose rates.

key_findings: Skin reaction analysis showed a trend toward tissue-sparing in FLASH-PT (268 Gy/s) versus CONV-PT (0.27 Gy/s) at 22.5 Gy single-dose proton SOBP irradiation.
No contrast enhancement was observed on MRI in either irradiated group over six months of follow-up.

Microglia activation density did not differ at the group level between FLASH-PT and CONV-PT, though both treatments increased activated microglia density relative to sham, with distinct regional increase in the periventricular area.
42181161.reviewer_note: This is a small pilot study (n=6 per irradiated group) explicitly framed as methodological, so the negative microglia finding should be read as endpoint-specific rather than a general refutation of dose-rate thresholds for sparing.
42181161.summary: This study irradiated the brains of C57BL/6JRj mice (partial brain, single fraction, 22.5 Gy, proton SOBP) comparing FLASH-PT (268 Gy/s, n=6) to CONV-PT (0.27 Gy/s, n=6) and unirradiated sham (n=2), with six-month follow-up. Skin reactions showed a trend toward tissue sparing in the FLASH-PT group as a short-term endpoint. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed no contrast enhancement in either irradiated group over the follow-up period. Histological assessment of microglia activation showed no group-level difference between FLASH-PT and CONV-PT, though both irradiated groups showed increased density of activated microglia relative to sham, most distinct in the periventricular area.

key_findings: MRC5-hTERT fibroblasts showed no significant difference in D10 survival values between VHEE (140.6 MeV) and CIEE (7 MeV) irradiation (P=.7)
Ex vivo mouse precision-cut lung slices showed dose-dependent decreases in cell division with no interbeam differences at 3, 6, or 9 Gy (P>.99)
Zebrafish embryos irradiated with 6 or 9 Gy showed dose-dependent body shortening and spinal curvature with no significant differences between VHEE and CIEE at matched doses (P≥.5)
42183317.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify dose rates for either the VHEE or CIEE beams, so it is unclear whether this study involves ultra-high dose rate delivery at all; the comparison appears focused on beam energy (VHEE vs conventional intermediate energy) rather than dose rate, and therefore does not directly engage with the registered FLASH-related claims. If dose rates were conventional for both arms, this paper may be tangential to the corpus's core UHDR focus despite its radiobiological multiscale design.
42183317.summary: This study compares radiobiological effects of laser-plasma-accelerated very high energy electrons (VHEE, mean energy 140.6 MeV) against conventional intermediate energy electrons (CIEE, 7 MeV linac) across three model systems: MRC5-hTERT human fibroblasts (2-10 Gy), mouse precision-cut lung slices (3, 6, 9 Gy), and zebrafish embryos (6 and 9 Gy). Endpoints included clonogenic-type viability survival curves, inhibition of cell replication in lung tissue, and developmental toxicity (body length, spinal curvature) in zebrafish. No significant differences were found between VHEE and CIEE for D10 values in fibroblasts (P=.7), cell division inhibition in lung slices at any dose (P>.99), or developmental toxicity metrics in zebrafish (P≥.5). The abstract does not report dose rates for either beam, so the comparison addresses beam energy/quality equivalence rather than ultra-high versus conventional dose rate effects.

key_findings: 1 GeV electron beams achieved the minimum FWHM and strongest focusing capability at the focal point among the three energies tested.
500 MeV beams showed only a limited increase in focal size and FWHM compared with 1 GeV beams.
200 MeV beams exhibited relatively poor focusing performance in deep regions of the water phantom.
500 MeV is proposed as a viable substitute for 1 GeV in specific clinical or engineering contexts, balancing dosimetric performance against implementation cost.
42214429.reviewer_note: This paper is primarily an accelerator/beam-optics design and transport optimization study using Monte Carlo simulation for dose distribution characterization, which fits Beam Delivery & Technology (engineering feasibility of UHDR delivery via focused electron beams) better than Modeling & Mechanisms, since the simulation is not modeling a FLASH mechanism (e.g., oxygen depletion, chemical kinetics) but rather beam transport/focusing physics for a novel delivery concept. No dose rate, biological, or clinical data are given, so no registered claims are addressed or contradicted.
42214429.summary: This modeling study uses Monte Carlo simulation (FLUKA) to characterize a focused electron beam transport system for deep-seated tumor FLASH radiotherapy, comparing 1 GeV, 500 MeV, and 200 MeV electron beams in a water phantom under the same optical configuration. The beam transport line was optimized to focus electrons at depth, and dose distributions including focal spot size and FWHM were quantitatively compared across energies. The 1 GeV beam achieved the smallest FWHM and strongest focusing at the focal point, while the 200 MeV beam showed relatively poor focusing performance in deep regions. The authors propose that a 500 MeV beam offers a practical balance between dosimetric performance and implementation cost relative to 1 GeV. No dose rate, biological endpoint, or dose delivery timing data are reported.

key_findings: Cell-sparing effect (increased surviving fraction, reduced gammaH2AX DNA damage) at 100 Gy/s versus 1 Gy/s was reproduced on a different carbon-ion scanning system at another facility using matched beam parameters (7 Gy, LETd 16.3 and 50 keV/micrometer).
HDF and Nuli-1 cell lines showed cell-sparing effects enhanced at higher LET (50 keV/micrometer) compared to lower LET (16.3 keV/micrometer).
HSGc-C5 showed a smaller cell-sparing effect than the other lines, with the effect absent at low LET.
Results support that the cell-sparing effect depends on beam parameters (dose, dose rate, LET, scanning pattern) rather than on the specific irradiation device.
42234857.reviewer_note: This is an in vitro cell-sparing (not whole-animal or tumor-endpoint) study using carbon-ion UHDR; it does not directly test in vivo normal-tissue sparing thresholds (BIO-002) or tumor control isoeffectiveness (BIO-003), so no direct contradiction is flagged, though the cross-facility device-independence finding is thematically relevant to reproducibility discussions in the corpus.
42234857.summary: This study used carbon-ion beam scanning at a second facility to test whether the in vitro cell-sparing effect depends on the irradiation device or on beam parameters. Human salivary gland cells (HSGc-C5), human dermal fibroblasts (HDF), and human lung bronchial epithelial cells (Nuli-1) were irradiated under normoxia at 7 Gy physical dose, with average dose rates of 100 Gy/s (ultra-high dose rate) versus 1 Gy/s (normal dose rate), at dose-averaged LET of 16.3 or 50 keV/micrometer, using scanning patterns matched to prior work. Colony formation assay and gammaH2AX immunofluorescence showed that HDF and Nuli-1 exhibited cell-sparing effects with increased surviving fraction and reduced DNA damage at ultra-high dose rate, with the effect enhanced at higher LET, while HSGc-C5 showed a smaller effect that was absent at low LET. The authors report these results as consistent with previous studies performed on a different machine, supporting the conclusion that the cell-sparing effect depends on beam parameters rather than the specific irradiation device used to deliver them.

key_findings: Proton FLASH (approximately 200 Gy/s, 11 Gy) preserved bone mineral density, bone volume fraction, and trabecular number compared with conventional dose-rate irradiation (0.2 Gy/s) in juvenile mice.
Tibial length ratios were 0.94 (FLASH) vs 0.91 (CONV) vs 1.00 (SHAM), indicating partial preservation of longitudinal bone growth with FLASH.
Bone marrow cellularity loss was smaller with FLASH (5.3% reduction vs SHAM) than with CONV (11.3% reduction; P < .05).
Muscle fibrosis positivity was lower with FLASH (2.6%) than CONV (3.0%; P < .05), with no severe immobility or weight loss across groups.
42235691.reviewer_note: This paper reports an in vivo tissue-endpoint FLASH sparing study in a juvenile mouse model at ~200 Gy/s proton irradiation, consistent with but not directly testing BIO-002's dose-rate threshold; it extends prior adult proton FLASH work to a pediatric skeletal/marrow context rather than contradicting existing claims.
42235691.summary: This study used juvenile C57BL/6 mice (3 to 4 weeks old) irradiated on the left hind leg with a synchrotron-based proton beamline, comparing 11 Gy proton FLASH (approximately 200 Gy/s) against conventional dose-rate irradiation (CONV, 0.2 Gy/s average) and sham treatment, with outcomes assessed 10 weeks post-treatment. FLASH preserved bone microarchitecture relative to CONV, with higher bone mineral density and bone volume fraction (P < .05), maintained trabecular number, and a structure model index indicating more favorable trabecular structure. Tibial length ratios were 0.94 for FLASH versus 0.91 for CONV versus 1.00 for SHAM, and bone marrow cellularity was reduced by 5.3% versus SHAM in FLASH mice compared with an 11.3% reduction in CONV mice (P < .05). Muscle fibrosis positivity was 2.6% in FLASH versus 3.0% in CONV (P < .05), and no severe immobility or weight loss was observed in any group.

key_findings: FLASH-RT (5.6x10^6 Gy/s) induced a distinct transcriptomic signature in CA3 and DG neurons compared to conventional dose rate (0.1 Gy/s), with upregulation of glutamate receptor genes, calcium signaling, LTP, and mitochondrial OXPHOS pathways.
AMPAR protein levels were increased at 48 hours post-FLASH in DG and CA3, with sustained elevation at 2 and 4 weeks.
Proposed mechanism links early calcium influx to durable AMPAR upregulation in CA3 neurons/progenitors as a candidate driver of long-term cognitive sparing after FLASH-RT.
42239092.reviewer_note: This paper addresses a normal-tissue (brain) molecular mechanism distinct from the oxygen-depletion mechanism referenced in MECH-001; it proposes an alternative or complementary neuroprotective pathway (AMPAR/glutamate signaling) rather than directly testing or contradicting oxygen depletion. No dose-rate threshold or timing data are given to compare against BIO-001/BIO-002. Abstract does not specify pulse structure details or beam type (electron vs other), limiting classification of delivery hardware context.
42239092.summary: This study used C57BL/6J mice receiving whole-brain irradiation with either 1 or 3 fractions of 10 Gy, delivered at ultra-high dose rate (5.6x10^6 Gy/s, single-pulse FLASH) or conventional dose rate (0.1 Gy/s). Spatial transcriptomics (Nanostring) identified a distinct transcriptomic signature in CA3 and dentate gyrus neurons after FLASH-RT, with upregulation of genes encoding glutamate receptors, calcium signaling, long-term potentiation, and mitochondrial OXPHOS pathways. Early transcriptional upregulation of Gria genes corresponded to increased AMPAR protein levels at 48 hours in the DG and CA3 regions, with elevated AMPAR expression sustained at 2 and 4 weeks post-irradiation. The authors propose that FLASH-RT-induced neuroprotection involves early calcium influx followed by sustained AMPAR expression in CA3 neurons and/or neural progenitors, potentially underlying long-term cognitive sparing.

key_findings: Electron FLASH (190 Gy/sec) reduced tongue ulceration and mucositis severity at 10 days post-irradiation compared to CONV (0.2 Gy/sec) in both WT (25 Gy) and Fanca-/- (18 Gy) mice
Histopathology showed decreased epithelial thinning and ulceration in FLASH-irradiated tongues relative to CONV
Fewer γ-H2AX foci at 12 hours post-irradiation in WT mice treated with FLASH versus CONV, with a similar trend in Fanca-/- mice
DNA-repair-deficient (Fanca-/-) mice, a model of heightened radiosensitivity, also exhibited reduced FLASH-associated toxicity
42244584.reviewer_note: Study addresses normal-tissue sparing only (non-tumor-bearing mice); it does not report tumor control data and therefore neither supports nor contradicts BIO-003. It also does not vary dose rate or fractionation timing, so it does not directly test BIO-002 or BIO-001 thresholds, though the 190 Gy/sec value used is consistent with the registered sparing range. Notable as an extension to a DNA-repair-deficient (Fanconi anemia) genetic background, which is a new model system context worth tracking even though it does not alter the underlying claims.
42244584.summary: This study compared electron beam FLASH (190 Gy/sec) and conventional dose rate (CONV, 0.2 Gy/sec) single-dose oral cavity irradiation in 129/Sv wild-type and Fanca-deficient (Fanconi anemia model) mice, using non-tumor-bearing animals to assess normal-tissue toxicity. Wild-type mice received 25 Gy and Fanca-/- mice received 18 Gy under each modality, with tongues harvested at 12 hours and 10 days post-irradiation. At 10 days post-irradiation, FLASH-treated tongues showed reduced dorsal surface ulceration and lower histopathological mucositis severity scores, with decreased epithelial thinning and ulceration, in both genetic backgrounds compared to CONV. At 12 hours post-irradiation, FLASH-treated wild-type mice showed fewer γ-H2AX foci than CONV-treated wild-type mice, with a similar trend reported in Fanca-/- mice.

key_findings: Ion radiography detector tracked a mock spherical tumour undergoing breathing-style motion to 0.1 mm accuracy
Imaging dose was approximately one third of comparable x-ray fluoroscopy methods
3D range modulator positioning was reproducible to 0.3 percent, though dynamic driving of the modulator is not yet possible
Real-time trigger-based gating from imaging to treatment was demonstrated with correct mock tumour positioning
Simulated quasi-static treatment achieved D95 percent of 98 percent (passive) and 99.2 percent (active) beam energy switching
42246123.reviewer_note: This paper addresses motion management and image guidance for conventional-dose-rate hadron therapy; it mentions FLASH only as a potential future application and does not report dose rates, dosimetry characterization, or biological endpoints relevant to the registered claims. No contradiction identified; the work is largely orthogonal to the existing corpus claims, which concern UHDR dosimetry, radiobiology, and clinical FLASH delivery specifically.
42246123.summary: This work develops the LIGHT concept, combining a plastic scintillator-based real-time ion radiography detector with a patient-specific 3D range modulator for lung cancer hadron therapy motion management. A 3 cm spherical plastic tumour undergoing breathing-style motion in a mock lung phantom was tracked to 0.1 mm accuracy, with imaging dose approximately one third of comparable x-ray fluoroscopy methods. Modulator positioning reproducibility was measured at 0.3 percent, and a real-time trigger-based switch from imaging to treatment was demonstrated with the mock tumour located at the expected position. An offline simulated dosimetric study reported D95 percent of 98 percent and 99.2 percent for passive and active beam energy switching respectively, compared against standard rescanning motion mitigation.

key_findings: An instantaneous dose rate of 10^8 Gy/s suppressed early O2•- formation and reduced steady-state H2O2 by ~12% relative to the independent-track approach, an effect attributed to intertrack interactions among OH•, e(aq)-, and H3O+, and diminished at 21% pO2.
A mean dose rate of 500 Gy/s enhanced H2O2 production to ~0.17 µM/Gy, a ~30% increase over ~0.12 µM/Gy at 0.28 Gy/s, consistently across oxygen levels at neutral pH.
The model predicts an increase in H2O2 with mean dose rate around 10^3 Gy/s, linked to OH• lifetime effects during the homogeneous chemical stage.
Dose-rate effects on H2O2 yield are jointly modulated by pH and initial oxygen concentration.
42248183.reviewer_note: This paper models H2O2 radiolytic chemistry and dose-rate/pH/oxygen interactions but does not directly assess radiolytic oxygen depletion magnitude or in vivo normal-tissue sparing, so it does not directly test MECH-001; it addresses a related but distinct radiochemical species/endpoint. Could be flagged as relevant context for future oxygen-depletion mechanism claims but not a direct contradiction or qualification here.
42248183.summary: This study uses TOPAS-nBio v2.0 Monte Carlo track-structure simulations coupled with a GillesPy2/ODE homogeneous chemistry module to model H2O2 production in water radiolysis across doses of 0.2-60 Gy, instantaneous dose rates up to ~10^8 Gy/s (10 ns FWHM pulse), and mean dose rates from 0.28 to 10^5 Gy/s, at pH 0.4-7 and initial oxygen levels of 1%, 4%, and 21% pO2. The model compares an independent-track (low dose-rate, 60Co-referenced) approach against pulsed irradiation to capture intertrack effects, and reproduces experimental H2O2 yields, oxygen dependence, single-pulse behavior, and pH dependence within 1 ± 0.5%. No specific tissue or tumour system is modeled; this is a purely physicochemical radiolysis simulation.

contradictions.explanation: The paper does not resolve the lack of consensus on dose-rate metrics but provides new empirical evidence favoring dose-averaged dose rate (DADR) as the metric most predictive of the biological FLASH effect, since multi-spill delivery preserved neuroprotection despite failing to qualify as FLASH under field dose rate or PBS dose rate definitions. This refines rather than contradicts the claim that the metrics are non-interchangeable.

The study reports neuroprotection preserved under multi-spill delivery with an approximately 2-second inter-spot delay, a temporal structure not captured by the mean dose rate threshold framework in BIO-002; this suggests mean/instantaneous dose rate alone may not determine sparing when spill structure and DADR are considered, refining the stated dose-rate threshold model.

key_findings: Multi-spill PBS delivery on a synchrotron, with ~2-second inter-spot delay, produced neuroprotection equivalent to single-spill PBS and passive scatter despite qualifying as FLASH only under the dose-averaged dose rate (DADR) metric, not field dose rate or PBS dose rate.

All three UHDR delivery techniques (single-spill PBS, multi-spill PBS, passive scatter) significantly preserved discrimination index on novel object recognition versus conventional dose rate at 10 Gy whole-brain irradiation.
FLASH-treated females showed preserved cognitive flexibility on touchscreen reversal learning versus conventional delivery.
Iba1+ microglia counts were reduced and morphology suggested preserved homeostatic state in FLASH versus conventional groups across techniques.
42282691.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify field dose rate or PBS dose rate numerical values, nor beam energy or proton range, limiting assessment of how these compare to conventional dose rate quantitatively. This is an animal (mouse) neurocognitive study, not a clinical trial, so it does not directly bear on CLIN-001.
42282691.summary: This study used C57BL/6 mice (7-8 weeks old) receiving 10 Gy whole-brain irradiation via a clinical Hitachi ProBEAT synchrotron proton system, comparing three transmission-beam ultra-high-dose-rate techniques (single-spill pencil beam scanning, multi-spill PBS with approximately 2-second inter-spot delay, and passive scatter) against conventional dose-rate delivery and unirradiated controls (n=24-28/group). Dose rate was characterized using three metrics: field dose rate, PBS dose rate, and dose-averaged dose rate (DADR); single-spill PBS and passive scatter met FLASH criteria under all three definitions, while multi-spill PBS qualified only under DADR. Despite this metric-dependent classification, novel object recognition testing at 6 weeks showed significantly higher discrimination index for all three FLASH techniques versus conventional delivery (single-spill PBS P=0.021, multi-spill PBS P=0.008, passive scatter P<0.001), with no significant difference among FLASH techniques. Touchscreen reversal learning at 14 weeks showed preserved cognitive flexibility in FLASH-treated females (P=0.047 vs. conventional), and Iba1+ microglia were reduced with morphology suggestive of a homeostatic state in FLASH-treated hippocampi.

key_findings: Measured beam-off latency was 56.7 µs (± 4.9 µs).
Radiofrequency optimization reduced DPP variability within the first five pulses from 26.7% to less than 0.5% for both conventional DPPs and UH-DPPs.
Total output decreased by up to 20% when VEXT voltage inputs deviated from the optimal solution by more than ± 10%.
Beam current transformer linearity was demonstrated from conventional DPPs to ultrahigh DPPs.
42284309.reviewer_note: This paper describes accelerator RF/beam control engineering rather than dosimetric measurement standards, chemical/biological mechanisms, or clinical outcomes, so it does not directly engage any registered claim. It could be cross-referenced with DOS-001/DOS-002 as supporting infrastructure for future dosimetric intercomparison work, but makes no dosimetric accuracy or standardization claims itself.
42284309.summary: This study describes an external beam control system (EBCS) for a modified clinical electron linear accelerator, designed to regulate dose per pulse (DPP) across conventional and ultra-high dose-per-pulse (UH-DPP) delivery over a 6-20 MeV energy range. The system uses radiofrequency power optimization via voltage inputs to the automatic frequency control interface, combined with real-time monitoring through either an internal transmission ion chamber or a multistage beam current transformer, and is interfaced with the accelerator's gating system. No tissue, cell, or beam quality/dose-rate irradiation endpoint is reported; the work is limited to characterization of beam control hardware performance.

key_findings: Solenoid focusing reduced the 80% isodose beam diameter from ~6 cm to ~2 cm.
Measured dose rate reached 125 Gy/s at 50 Hz repetition frequency.
Focused beam FWHM measured as 1.26 cm (X) and 1.39 cm (Y).
TOPAS Monte Carlo simulation agreed with EBT-XD film dosimetry to within ~4% in the high-dose region.
Scanning-magnet steering produced tunable three-spot patterns with peak-to-peak spacing up to ~2.9 cm and peak-to-valley dose ratio up to 28.0.
