42582154.summary: This in vitro study compared MCF10A (non-tumorigenic) and MDA-MB-231 (triple-negative) breast cell lines irradiated with electron beams at 2, 4, 6, 9, 11, and 15 Gy delivered at FLASH (230 Gy/s) or CONV (6 Gy/min) dose rates under normoxic conditions. Clonogenic survival curves were comparable between FLASH and CONV in both cell lines. Early DNA damage markers showed a dose-rate effect: increased γ-H2AX foci at 1 hour post-FLASH-RT in both lines and greater persistence of 53BP1 foci at 24 hours in MDA-MB-231 cells. Transcriptomic profiling at 24 hours (9 and 15 Gy) showed broader gene modulation after FLASH-RT, with mitochondrial gene upregulation in MCF10A and structural gene induction in MDA-MB-231, while Luminex-based immunological profiling and GSH/GSSG ratio measurements at 24 hours showed no qualitative dose-rate differences, though MDA-MB-231 produced higher levels of several immune factors after FLASH-RT.

key_findings: Four-ring double-scattering system achieves 53±2% transmission with ±3% dose homogeneity, exceeding tenfold improvement over single scattering
Configuration delivers a dose rate of 77 Gy/s at 100 nA for a 30 mm field size, exceeding commonly cited FLASH dose-rate thresholds
Mathematical optimization model reproduces prior two-ring results (Takada 1994) and extends to three- and four-ring systems
TOPAS Monte Carlo and Bragg-peak measurements confirm distal penumbra below 1 mm and water-range agreement within 0.1 mm
42608218.reviewer_note: This paper concerns passive beam-shaping hardware (scattering ring optimization) for ocular proton therapy, not a mechanistic or biological model of the FLASH effect, so it is classified as Beam Delivery & Technology despite the keyword-model tag of Modeling & Mechanisms. The reported 77 Gy/s dose rate is a beam-delivery capability metric and does not itself test or contradict BIO-002's biological dose-rate threshold claim, since no tissue or tumour endpoint is reported.
42608218.summary: This study develops a mathematical optimization framework for designing multiple-ring double-scattering systems for a 70 MeV cyclotron used in ocular proton therapy at HZB, aiming to maximize beam transmission under a field-homogeneity constraint. A Python GUI implements the optimization for two- to four-ring configurations, incorporating energy degradation, range shifting, and conversion of scattering angles to physical ring dimensions. The four-ring design achieved 53±2% transmission with ±3% dose homogeneity, corresponding to a dose rate of 77 Gy/s at 100 nA for a 30 mm field, exceeding commonly cited FLASH dose-rate thresholds. Bragg-peak measurements and TOPAS Monte Carlo simulations confirmed a distal penumbra below 1 mm and water-range agreement within 0.1 mm of predictions. The four-ring system increased transmission more than tenfold relative to single scattering.

key_findings: Bio-RMs optimized with mMKM and LEM1 achieved measured survival fractions within 5% of model predictions across biological SOBPs of 4 and 8 Gy(RBE) in a non-small cell lung cancer cell line.
Physical dose measurements agreed with Monte Carlo calculations within 1.2%.
Secondary fragment analysis showed bio-RMs increased the relative contribution of light and intermediate fragments.

In retrospective clinical planning for vertebral metastasis and lung tumor cases, bio-RM plans matched IMPT target coverage and OAR metrics with slightly reduced homogeneity and reduced estimated delivery times from minutes to seconds.
Robustness analysis under manufacturing, setup, and range uncertainties showed acceptable plan stability.
42624158.reviewer_note: This paper addresses conventional-dose-rate carbon ion RBE-optimized treatment planning and range-modulator hardware; it does not report UHDR delivery, dose-rate metrics, or FLASH biological endpoints, so it does not engage the registered dosimetry, mechanism, or biology claims directly. It is included in the corpus only as a stated future basis for UHDR/motion-management studies at synchrotron facilities.
42624158.summary: This study develops patient-specific 3D range modulators (bio-RMs) for carbon ion therapy that are optimized for RBE-weighted biological effect rather than physical dose, using the modified microdosimetric kinetic model and local effect model 1, with cell-line-specific mMKM parameters derived for a non-small cell lung cancer line. Bio-RMs designed for 4 and 8 Gy(RBE) biological spread-out Bragg peaks were 3D printed and validated with clonogenic assays, showing measured survival fractions within 5% of mMKM predictions and physical dose measurements within 1.2% of Monte Carlo calculations. Comparative treatment planning for vertebral metastasis and lung tumor cases showed bio-RM plans achieved target coverage and OAR metrics comparable to reference IMPT, with slightly reduced target homogeneity, and estimated delivery times reduced from minutes to seconds by eliminating energy switching. Robustness analyses indicated acceptable stability under manufacturing, setup, and range uncertainties evaluated. The work is framed as a basis for future motion-management and ultra-high-dose-rate studies at synchrotron-based facilities but does not itself report UHDR delivery or dose-rate-dependent biological effects.

key_findings: SEBP-FLASH achieved superior conformity index (1.4 ± 0.2) versus robotic radiosurgery (1.9 ± 0.3, p=0.001), with comparable GI50/GI30 gradient indices.
Brain V40 Gy/s dose-rate coverage exceeded 80% under a 5 Gy dose threshold and 400 minimum monitor unit setting.
SEBP-FLASH field delivery time was under 1 second per field, proposed to reduce on-table time versus robotic delivery.
42630800.reviewer_note: This is a dosimetric/planning feasibility comparison, not a clinical outcome or radiobiological study, despite the keyword-model tag of Radiobiology. No patient outcomes, toxicity, or biological endpoints are reported, so it does not engage CLIN-001 or the biological sparing claims (BIO-001/002/003). The use of a specific V40 Gy/s dose-rate coverage metric with defined dose threshold and MU cutoff is consistent with, rather than contradicting, PLAN-001's observation of multiple non-interchangeable dose-rate metric definitions in use.
42630800.summary: This planning study re-optimized recurrent glioblastoma reirradiation cases originally treated with robotic image-guided stereotactic radiosurgery, using a single-energy Bragg-peak proton FLASH (SEBP-FLASH) technique with patient-specific apertures. Plan quality metrics (GTV coverage, conformity index, GI50/GI30, DVHs) were compared between SEBP-FLASH and the robotic technique, with SEBP-FLASH achieving a conformity index of 1.4 ± 0.2 versus 1.9 ± 0.3 for the robotic system (p=0.001) and comparable gradient indices (GI50 2.9 ± 0.5 vs 2.7 ± 0.2, p=0.085; GI30 6.2 ± 1.8 vs 5.5 ± 0.5, p=0.189). Using a dose threshold of 5 Gy and minimum monitor unit of 400, brain V40 Gy/s dose-rate coverage exceeded 80%. Each SEBP-FLASH field was delivered in under 1 second, with the study reporting feasibility and reduced on-table time relative to the robotic technique rather than any measured biological or clinical outcome.
